articles.title: Does a low resting heart rate actually cause antisocial behavior?
articles.summary: Using genetic data from thousands of twins, researchers have challenged a long-held psychological theory. They found little evidence that resting heart rate causes antisocial behavior, pointing instead to sensation seeking as a key target for behavioral therapies.

articles.title: RBS-Attention: Radius-Bounded Sparse Prefill for Long-Context Large Language Models
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.20971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context large language model inference is increasingly limited by prefill, where dense self-attention processes the entire prompt before generation begins. Sparse block selection can reduce this cost, but a block centroid may hide a highly relevant token among many irrelevant ones. We call this failure mode mean dilution and propose RBS-Attention, a training-free sparse-prefill method with two complementary selection branches. articles.title: Attention-Aware Routing: Coupling Routing and Attention in MoEs
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.20974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts language models, the router typically selects and weights experts based on the token's hidden state, utilizing limited contextual information. We propose Attention-Aware Routing (AAR), which augments the router with temporal and spectral features extracted from a sliding window of attention weights that represent a summary of the model's contextual state, disentangled from the hidden state. articles.title: CaLR: Causal Latent Revision for Robust Diffusion Reasoning
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.20981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models suffer from local greediness, while diffusion language models (DLMs) often lack the strict causal structure required for reasoning. To combine the advantages and overcome the drawbacks of the dual, we propose Causal Latent Revision (CaLR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as constrained latent optimization. By adopting a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and implicit differentiation, CaLR performs gradient-guided ``thought revision" to enforce logical consistency, enabling dynamic self-correction

articles.title: People with low implicit self-worth are quicker to notice subtle facial cues of anger and disgust
articles.summary: People with hidden doubts about their self-worth are quicker to spot subtle facial expressions of anger and disgust. New research shows that unconscious self-esteem strongly influences how we perceive social cues and navigate relationships.

articles.title: Scientists trace the nerve pathway that links digestion to memory
articles.summary: A new small study in rats reveals that the digestive tract communicates with the brain during meals to help remember where food was found, a process that can be disrupted by an early-life junk food diet.

articles.title: Why do people protest? Six decades of research points to social connections over personal grievances
articles.summary: A comprehensive review of 60 years of research reveals that people who participate in protests are driven more by social connections and political interest than by personal grievances, anger, or mistrust of the government.

articles.title: Autism is linked to a nearly 14-year shorter life expectancy among Medicaid beneficiaries
articles.summary: A new study indicates that autistic individuals on Medicaid have a life expectancy nearly 14 years shorter than the general U.S. population. This stark gap is largely driven by preventable causes like infections, malnutrition, and fatal accidents.

articles.title: Psilocybin and standard antidepressants both shift the brain away from negative biases
articles.summary: A new study reveals that psilocybin and standard antidepressants both reduce the brain's tendency to misinterpret facial expressions as negative. The research suggests these two distinct treatments share a common cognitive effect in the fight against depression.
